query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A nanocrystalline, Cu-containing refractory high-entropy alloy (specifically a CuMoTaWV film) deposited on a copper matrix will improve the surface wear resistance by forming a strong metallurgical bond and providing a graded, high‐hardness barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk copper substrate with a relatively smooth but unprotected surface.
generation.intervention: Deposit a nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV high-entropy alloy coating via a process such as DC magnetron sputtering to adhere it onto the copper substrate.
generation.conditions: Wear testing under room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures (e.g., up to 300 °C) using reciprocating wear or sliding tests to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanocrystalline microstructure (grain sizes ~18 nm) of the HEA film, along with the graded interface formed by the shared copper element, enhances bonding and mechanical integration at the surface.
generation.mechanism: The high hardness and refined grain structure of the HEA coating reduce the wear depth by acting as a barrier against mechanical abrasion. Moreover, the presence of copper in the alloy improves chemical compatibility and minimizes thermal expansion mismatch, leading to a strong, adherent interface with the Cu matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated copper substrate will exhibit significantly lower wear rates and reduced coefficient of friction compared to an uncoated copper surface, thereby enhancing the overall durability and service life of the component.
generation.baseline: Wear resistance and surface performance of a bare Cu substrate tested under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects may diminish if the thermal or mechanical loading conditions induce interfacial stresses (beyond approximately 300 °C or under extreme cyclic loading) that could challenge the adhesion between the HEA coating and the Cu matrix.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of wear resistance improvement and long-term stability of the interfacial bond under various thermal cycling conditions remain uncertain and require further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of copper substrates: one set with the DC-magnetron-sputtered CuMoTaWV HEA coating and one set left uncoated. Subject both sets to reciprocating wear tests at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (e.g., 300 °C) under identical load and sliding conditions. Evaluate the wear depth, coefficient of friction, and examine the interfacial integrity using microscopy and scratch tests.
measurements: Interfacial adhesion strength (measured via scratch testing)
Microstructural characterization of the coating/substrate interface (via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the copper substrate with the HEA coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in wear depth and friction, and if the interfacial adhesion is not demonstrably stronger than that of the uncoated substrate under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
